title: Keeping farrowing and litter records for pigs
subtitle: What to record at each farrowing and why it pays off at selection time.
excerpt: Farrowing records are the basic evidence base for improving your pig herd. Without records, you are guessing which sows produce the most viable litters, which have weaning problems, and which carry genetics that are improving your weights. With three years of records, selection becomes straightforward: keep daughters of your best producers, cull the tail of your worst. This tutorial covers exactly what to record at each farrowing and how to use it.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork, Pig Farrowing Records and Performance Indicators (2022). NPA (National Pig Association), Smallholder Pig Keeping Guide (2022). John Gadd, Pig Production Problems (2011), 5m Books. DEFRA, Pig identification and movement regulations guidance (2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: The act of giving birth in pigs. A sow that is about to give birth is described as being due to farrow. The farrowing rate (proportion of matings that produce a litter) and litter size are the two most important commercial performance indicators.

The count of piglets that show signs of life at birth, regardless of whether they survive the first day. Distinguished from stillborn (dead at birth) and mummified piglets (that died and desiccated in utero).
The number of days from weaning a litter until the sow is re-mated (served). A short interval (under 7 days) indicates good sow body condition and reproductive health.

content.text: A farrowing record is a note made at each
farrowing
of the data you need to evaluate the sow, the service (mating), and the litter. It takes five minutes to fill in at the time; reconstructing it later from memory is impossible.
What to record at farrowing
Sow tag number and name (if named).
Boar used, and date of service or AI.
Date and time of first piglet, date and time of last piglet.
Count of
born alive
, stillborn, and mummified.
Any help needed at birth, and whether a vet was involved.
Sow body condition score at farrowing (1 to 5 scale, where 3 is ideal).
What to record at weaning
Date of weaning.
Number of piglets weaned (piglets alive at weaning, not necessarily the same as born alive).
Average weaning weight (total litter weight divided by number weaned) if you have scales.
Date of re-service (
weaning to service interval
Any sow health notes: mastitis, metritis, lameness, poor appetite.
Simple record format

A single A4 page per sow per year works well in a smallholder context. Columns: litter number, service date, boar, expected farrow date, actual farrow date, born alive, stillborn, mummies, weaned alive, weaning date, weaning weight, re-service date. Keep the sheets in a folder per sow.
Using records for selection

Average born alive per litter across all litters is the most useful single number. A sow averaging 10 or more born alive per litter on a UK commercial cross is performing well. An outdoor-breed (Tamworth, Large Black, Berkshire) averaging 7 to 8 per litter is also strong for the breed type.
Flag any sow with two consecutive litters below 7 born alive, or with a pattern of high stillborn count, for culling consideration.
Retain gilts from the sow's best litter (highest born alive plus highest weaning weight). This compounds improvement over successive generations.

attrs.cue: High stillborn count in multiple consecutive litters from the same sow
attrs.cause: Prolonged farrowing (more than 4 to 5 hours), large litter size beyond the sow's capacity, or possible infectious cause
attrs.fix: Check the duration of the farrowing. A farrowing that takes over 4 hours significantly increases stillborn risk from hypoxia. If farrowing duration is normal, ask your vet to investigate for porcine reproductive causes.
